scenes.text: Plug in your phone at 3 a.m. Then plug it into the same outlet at 3 p.m. Same wall, same wires.
But depending on where you live, the power plants on the other end can be completely different. At night, maybe a wind farm on the plains. In the afternoon, solar panels that were dark at 3 a.m.
Stick with me, and you'll see why, in sunny states, the toughest hour for the grid often isn't the hottest one. And why, some days, power plants pay to give their electricity away.
Because the grid isn't one machine. It's a different machine every hour. So let's follow one day, hour by hour.

Let's start in the dark. According to the Energy Information Administration, U.S. electricity use typically bottoms out around five in the morning, when most people are asleep and most offices are closed.
scenes.graphic: line chart: typical U.S. hourly electricity demand over 24 hours, low point near 5 a.m.

scenes.text: But it never drops to zero. Refrigerators and other always-on devices keep running, and the EIA calls that steady floor of demand baseload.
The classic baseload plant is nuclear. It's cheap to run once it's built, so operators try to keep it at full power around the clock.

In 2025, the average U.S. nuclear plant ran at 91 percent of its maximum possible output, higher than any other kind of power plant. Nuclear supplied about 18 percent of the country's utility-scale electricity that year.
scenes.graphic: flat line chart: nuclear output across 24 hours vs. curved demand line

scenes.text: Now add the wind. In the middle of the country, the EIA says land-based wind is usually strongest overnight.

Take the Southwest Power Pool, the grid operator for a big stretch of the Great Plains. We ran its 2025 numbers from the EIA's hourly grid data: on average, wind output equaled about 46 percent of demand at 2 a.m., but only about 31 percent at noon. And for five straight hours before dawn on December 28, 2025, it equaled about 80 percent.
scenes.graphic: line chart: SPP 2025 average wind share of demand by hour of day (Central time), ~46% at 2 a.m. vs ~31% at noon; callout 'Dec 28, 2025: ~80% for 5 hours before dawn'; source note 'EIA Hourly Electric Grid Monitor (EIA-930), our calculation'

scenes.text: Some nights there's more wind than anyone needs, so operators turn turbines down to keep supply matched to demand.
Twelve hours later, the machine looks completely different. The sun is high, air conditioners are running, and in a growing number of places, solar is doing the heavy lifting.
Take Texas. In the summer of 2025, solar plants on the main Texas grid averaged 24 gigawatts between noon and one p.m. Two summers earlier, it was 12.
scenes.graphic: bar chart: ERCOT average solar output at noon, summer 2023 (12 GW) vs. summer 2025 (24 GW)

scenes.text: Natural gas made room for it. Gas supplied half of the Texas grid's midday power in the summer of 2023, and 37 percent in the summer of 2025.

California has gone even further. Solar now supplies almost half of the grid operator's demand between eight in the morning and four in the afternoon, and in the first five months of 2026, it out-generated natural gas on 82 percent of days.
Now here's the twist I promised. You'd think the toughest moment for the grid is the hottest afternoon. But in places with lots of solar, it's often the stretch around sunset.

To see why, grid operators look at net load: total demand minus whatever wind and solar are producing. It's the part every other power plant has to cover. One catch: this counts only big solar farms and wind farms. Rooftop panels don't show up as supply at all. They just make demand look smaller.
scenes.graphic: diagram: total demand minus wind and solar equals net load, stacked area illustration

scenes.text: Plot net load over a typical day in California and it sags deep in the middle, then shoots up steeply in the evening. It looks like the outline of a duck, so it's called the duck curve. And the EIA says the belly keeps getting deeper as solar grows.
scenes.graphic: line chart: CAISO net load on a typical spring day, duck-shaped curve with belly at midday and steep neck at sunset

scenes.text: In spring, when demand is low, the belly can hold more solar than the grid can use. In 2024, California's grid operator curtailed 3.4 million megawatt-hours of wind and solar, and 93 percent of it was solar.
Then comes the neck. As solar fades around sunset, people get home, cook dinner and turn on lights and air conditioners. Everything that isn't the sun has to ramp up fast.
One fast-growing answer is a battery. Charge it with cheap midday solar, then let it run in the evening. As the EIA puts it, that flattens the duck's curve and shortens its neck.

And the scale has changed fast. California's grid operator reported that in 2025, batteries in its market delivered about 9,100 megawatts on average in the hour ending at 8 p.m. In 2024, it was about 5,700.
scenes.graphic: line chart: average battery charging (midday, negative) and discharging (evening, positive) by hour, CAISO 2024 vs. 2025

scenes.text: Which brings us to price. On the wholesale market, where power is bought and sold in bulk, electricity can cost wildly different amounts from one hour to the next.

Berkeley Lab found that the average wholesale price across the major U.S. power markets in 2023 was 36 dollars per megawatt-hour. But that average hides huge swings: in Texas, hourly prices on some summer evenings topped 500 dollars, and in California, on sunny spring days, they dropped below zero.
scenes.graphic: two heat maps (LBNL ReWEP 2023, regional average hourly price by day x hour): ERCOT with >$500 summer-evening hours in pink; CAISO with sub-zero sunny spring hours in light blue

scenes.text: Below zero. That's the strange part I promised at the start. A negative price means sellers are paying buyers to take their power.

Why would anyone do that? Some plants can't easily or cheaply shut down for a short stretch. Nuclear operators try to run at full power, and big steam plants face costs every time they stop and restart.
And some wind farms earn a tax credit for every megawatt-hour they produce. For a short stretch, paying a little beats shutting down.

In California's day-ahead market, prices were negative about 7 percent of the time in 2025, according to the grid operator's own market monitor. And Berkeley Lab found that in 2023, those negative prices showed up almost entirely in sunny hours of late spring and early summer.
scenes.graphic: bar chart: share of negative-price intervals in CAISO day-ahead market, 2024 (8.8%) vs. 2025 (7.1%)

scenes.text: On the other end are the expensive hours, when the grid calls on peakers, often gas turbines that run only occasionally. They cost more to run, but they respond quickly, which is exactly what that evening ramp needs.
So what does this mean at your house? Most of us never see wholesale prices, but your timing still matters.

Most electric vehicle drivers charge overnight at home, according to the Department of Energy. And some utilities offer time-of-use rates, where electricity costs less in certain hours and more in others.
That works because most homes now have smart meters that record use at least hourly. In 2022, about 73 percent of U.S. residential meters were smart meters, the EIA reports.

And here's where the old advice breaks down. On California's wholesale market, some of the cheapest hours are now in the middle of the day, not the middle of the night. So read your own utility's rate plan instead of guessing.
Running the dishwasher or charging the car in a cheap hour isn't just about your bill. It helps the grid fill the duck's belly instead of its neck.
Quick recap. At 3 a.m., demand is near its low, nuclear runs flat out, and on the Great Plains, wind is often at its strongest.
At 3 p.m., solar carries more and more of the load, sometimes enough to push prices below zero. Then at sunset comes the steep neck of the duck, and batteries and gas plants race to cover it.
The grid isn't one machine. It's a different machine every hour. And now you know how to read it.
So what does your utility charge at night versus in the afternoon? Do you have a time-of-use rate, or one flat price? Tell me your state in the comments.

meta.description:
At 3 a.m. and 3 p.m., the same outlet in your wall can be fed by completely different power plants.
We follow one day on the U.S. grid, hour by hour: wind and nuclear at night, solar at midday, and the steep evening ramp in between.

In this video:
- Why U.S. electricity demand bottoms out before dawn, and what baseload means
- Nuclear running flat out, and why Great Plains wind peaks overnight
- How solar took over the middle of the day in Texas and California
- Net load and the duck curve, explained simply
- Batteries shifting midday solar into the evening
- Why wholesale prices swing, and how they can go negative
- Why your timing (EV charging, time-of-use rates) matters
